the use of a strict protocol for the management of patients undergoing intracranial procedures is associated with a significant reduction in the rate of postoperative haematomas.
postoperative haematomas are not caused by abrupt rises in blood pressure.

postoperative intracranially located haematomas are a serious complication of craniotomy with a mortality of around 30% which is preventable by a strict anaesthesiologic protocol based on deep analgesia and a prolonged emergence from general anaesthesia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
postoperative haemorrhage is a preventable complication of intracraneal surgery.
the incidence of postoperative intracranially placed haematoma is virtually zero if a strict anaesthesiology protocol is used during and immediately after surgery.

1) postoperative clot formation is probably an avoid able complication of intracerebral surgery; and 2) it is possible to eliminate the risk of clot formation in a high percentage of patients if the anaesthesiologist follows a protocol of deep opioid anaesthesia, and the surgical team is prepared to wait for a prolonged time for the patient to emerge from anaesthesia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
postoperative intracranium haematoma is an avoidable complication.
it is possible to avoid postoperative intracranially haematoma by avoiding acute elevations of arterial pressure during and after the procedure.

postoperative haemorrhagic complications can be avoided in neurosurgical patients if the arterial pressure does not exceed 120 mmHg during the operation and if emergence from anaesthesia is delayed for at least 1 1.5 hours after craniotomy has been completed.
